Belgium has transposed ATAD 2 as well as the directive of 8 July 2014 amending the PSD. The rules adopted in Belgium in view of those transpositions are similar to those recommended in the reports "Neutralising the effects of branch mismatch arrangements" and "Neutralising the effects of hybrid mismatch arrangements". The following rules adopted in Belgium are similar to those recommended in the report "Neutralising the effects of branch mismatch arrangements": 
1) Denial of the exemption for income attributable to a disregarded PE (recommendation 1). 
2) Non-deductibility of a payment made to an entity with one or more PE, if not included in the taxable income of the payee as a result of differences in the allocation of payment between the head office and PE or between two or more PE of the same entity (recommendation 2 1 a). 
3) Non-deductibility of a payment made to a disregarded PE (recommendation 2 1 b). 
4) Non-deductibility of a deemed payment between the PE and the head office or between two PE, if not included in the taxable income of the payee (recommendation 3). 
5) Non-deductibility, in the hands of the parent, of a payment made by a hybrid PE, if deductible in the payer jurisdiction (recommendation 4 1 a). 
6) Non-deductibility of a payment, in the hands of the payer, of a payment made by a hybrid PE, if deductible in the parent jurisdiction (recommendation 4 1 b). 
7) Non-deductibility of a payment that funds directly or indirectly deductible expenditure giving rise to a hybrid mismatch, except to the extent that one of the other jurisdictions involved has made an equivalent adjustment in respect of such hybrid mismatch (recommendation 5). 
8) Denial of tax transparency for reverse hybrids (recommendation 5 2), except for CIV's. 
9) Non-deductibility, in the hands of the parent, of a payment made by a hybrid entity, if deductible in the payer jurisdiction (recommendation 6 1 a). 
10) Non-deductibility, in the hands of the payer, of a payment made by a hybrid entity, if deductible in the parent jurisdiction (recommendation 6 1 b). 
11) Non-deductibility of a payment made by a company which is a resident of Belgium and of another jurisdiction, if deductible in this other jurisdiction (recommendation 7). If both jurisdictions are EU Member States, the payment remains deductible if the company is deemed to be a resident of Belgium according to the tax treaty in force between the two EU Member States. 
12) Non-deductibility of a payment that funds directly or indirectly deductible expenditure giving rise to a hybrid mismatch, except to the extent that one of the other jurisdictions involved has made an equivalent adjustment in respect of such hybrid mismatch (recommendation 8).

The purpose of the first set of rules is to neutralize the effects of:
- Payments under a hybrid financial instrument that gives rise to a deduction/non-inclusion mismatch, including rules for D/NIs arising from a hybrid transfer of a financial instrument and from a substitute payment in respect of a financial instrument.

Section 4k of the German Income Tax Act (EStG) was introduced effective January 1, 2020, and neutralizes the effects of hybrid mismatch arrangements in the form of a linking rule. The regulation implements the binding provisions of Article 9 and 9b of the EU Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD I and II) against hybrid mismatches, which are based on the recommendations for preventing D/NI-, DD- and imported mismatches described in Part I of the final report on BEPS Action 2.
Section 4k of the German Income Tax Act limits the deductibility of payments in various situations of hybrid mismatch arrangements. The personal scope of application includes transactions between related parties (shareholding of at least 25%), permanent establishments, and structured arrangements. Section 4k of the German Income Tax Act is not limited to corporations but also applies to natural persons and to the taxation of partners in a transparent partnership.
Additionally, Section 8b Paragraph 1 Sentence 3 of the German Corporate Tax Act (KStG) was amended to include a regulation denying dividend exemption for hybrid transfers of financial instruments.
In 2017, as a result of the recommendations on BEPS Action 2, a special provision was introduced in Section 4i of the German Income Tax Act (EStG) to neutralise DD inconsistencies in the taxation of partnerships, which prevents double deductions of payments in certain cross-border constellations. Since the introduction of Section 4k EStG, the scope of application of this provision has also been largely covered by this provision.

Article 7.1 (Hybrid Mismatches) of the Enterprise Income Tax Law provides: 
- If the consequences of a hybrid mismatch are double deduction, then:
1) if the Republic of Latvia is the investor jurisdiction, the taxpayer shall increase the taxable base by the amount of deduction which has been deducted from the taxable income also abroad.
2) if the Republic of Latvia is the disburser jurisdiction, however, the taxable base has not been increased by the amount of deduction in the investor jurisdiction for the purposes of taxation, the taxpayer shall increase the taxable base by the amount of deduction;
3) the taxpayer has the right to reduce the dual inclusion income occurring in a taxation or post-taxation period for any such deduction.
- If the consequences of a hybrid mismatch are deduction without inclusion :
1) and if the Republic of Latvia is the disburser jurisdiction, the taxpayer shall increase the taxable base by the amount of deduction which has not been appropriately taken into account for determination of the taxable income abroad for the purposes of taxation;
2) and if the Republic of Latvia is the payee jurisdiction and the taxable base has not been increased by the amount of deduction abroad, the taxpayer shall increase the taxable base by the amount of income which was not taken into account when calculating the taxable income;
 - In addition, law provides: 
Hybrid Mismatches & Deductible Payments:
The taxable base is increased by any payment that leads to a hybrid mismatch (e.g. double deduction or deduction with no inclusion) between associated enterprises or within a structured arrangement — unless another jurisdiction has already made an equivalent adjustment.
Disregarded Permanent Establishments (PEs):
Income from a disregarded foreign PE must be included in the Latvian tax base, unless an applicable tax treaty with a non-EU country exempts it.
Hybrid Transfers (e.g. financial instruments):
If a tax rebate (e.g. withholding tax relief) is claimed by multiple parties, Latvia limits the taxpayer’s rebate to the portion of net taxable income actually earned.
Hybrid Entities with Foreign Ownership:
A Latvian hybrid entity (transparent for Latvian tax) may be treated as a tax resident if it is 50%+ owned by non-residents from countries that treat it as a taxable person, and the income is otherwise not taxed elsewhere. This does not apply to regulated collective investment undertakings.
Dual Resident Entities & Double Deductions:
If a taxpayer is a resident in both Latvia and another country, and deductions are claimed in both, Latvia increases the taxable base unless the other country offsets the double deduction with dual-inclusion income. If both countries are EU Member States, and the taxpayer is deemed non-resident in Latvia under a tax treaty, the adjustment still applies.

Article 28, Section XXIII of the Income Tax Law establishes that payments made to related parties or through a structured agreement are not deductible when the counterparty's income is subject to preferential tax regimes. New Section 267A -- Certain related party amounts paid or accrued in hybrid 
transactions or with hybrid entities. Section 267A of the Internal Revenue Code provides rules that neutralize certain hybrid mismatches, in order to prevent certain DD outcomes, D/NI outcomes, and indirect D/NI outcomes. Section 267A provides (or, in conjunction with regulations that could in the future be issued thereunder, could provide) results consistent with the BEPS Action Item 2 Report, Recommendation 1 (primary rule), Recommendation 3 (primary rule), Recommendation 4, and Recommendation 8, to the extent a hybrid mismatch would otherwise exist as a result of interest or royalties paid or accrued to related parties. Section 267A generally denies a deduction for the amount of interest or royalty paid or accrued to a related party if (i) in the payee jurisdiction, either the amount is not included in the related partys income or the related party is allowed a deduction for the amount, and (ii) the amount is paid or accrued pursuant to a hybrid transaction or by or to a hybrid entity. For this purpose, a hybrid transaction means any transaction, series of transactions, agreement, or instrument giving rise to a payment that is treated as interest or a royalty for U.S. tax purposes but is not so treated for foreign tax purposes. In addition, a hybrid entity is an entity that either is transparent for U.S. tax purposes but opaque for foreign tax purposes, or is opaque for U.S. tax purposes but transparent for foreign tax purposes. Section 267A broadly authorizes regulations to, among other things, (i) address certain conduit arrangement (e.g., imported mismatches), (ii) address certain structured transactions, (iii) disqualify the entire amount of interest or royalty if subject to a participation exemption system or other system which provides for the exclusion or deduction of a substantial porrtion of such amount, and (iv) apply the rules of section 267A to branches or U.S. entities. Proposed Regulations. The Treasury Department and the Internal Revenue Service are currently working on proposed regulations to implement section 267A and section 245A(e). The goal is to issue most proposed guidance implementing the new tax reform provisions by the end of the calendar year.

The anti-hybrid rules follow Articles 9, 9a and 9b of the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD). ATAD is fully aligned with the OECD BEPS Action 2 Report. The rules neutralising hybrid mismatch arrangements are set out in Articles 47f-47j of the Corporate Income Tax Act (CITA) and in Article 2, paragraphs 4-5 of CITA.

The rules cover hybrid mismatches that arise between the head office and permanent establishment or between two or more permanent establishments of the same entity, hybrid mismatches that arise between the taxpayer and its associated enterprises or between associated enterprises, and those resulting from a structured arrangement involving a taxpayer.

The rules address four categories of hybrid mismatches: first, hybrid mismatches that result from payments under a financial instrument; second, hybrid mismatches that are the consequence of differences in the allocation of payments made to a hybrid entity or permanent establishment, including as a result of payments to a disregarded permanent establishment; third, hybrid mismatches that result from payments made by a hybrid entity to its owner, or deemed payments between the head office and permanent establishment or between two or more permanent establishments; and last, double deduction outcomes resulting from payments made by a hybrid entity or permanent establishment.

In respect of payments under a financial instrument, a hybrid mismatch arises where the deduction without inclusion outcome is attributable to the differences in the characterisation of the instrument or the payments made under it. A deductible payment under a financial instrument that is not included in income by the payee within 12 months after the end of the tax period of the payer is treated as giving rise to a hybrid mismatch. 

In respect of payments made to a hybrid entity or permanent establishment, a hybrid mismatch arises where the deduction without inclusion outcome results from differences in the rules governing the allocation of that payment between the hybrid entity and its owner in the case of a payment that is made to a hybrid entity, between the head office and permanent establishment, or between two or more permanent establishments in the case of a deemed payment to a permanent establishment. There is a hybrid mismatch only where the mismatch outcome is a result of differences in the rules governing the allocation of payments under the laws of the two jurisdictions.

The rules also capture deduction without inclusion outcomes that are the result of payments made to a disregarded permanent establishment. A disregarded permanent establishment is any arrangement that is treated as giving rise to a permanent establishment under the laws of the head office jurisdiction but which is not treated as a permanent establishment under the laws of the other jurisdiction. 

In respect of payments made by a hybrid entity to its owner, or deemed payments made between the head office and permanent establishment or between two or more permanent establishments, a hybrid mismatch arises where the deduction without inclusion outcome results from the payment or deemed payment not being recognised in the payee jurisdiction. No hybrid mismatch arises where the payee is exempt from tax under the laws of the payee jurisdiction. In respect of this category of hybrid mismatches a mismatch outcome only arises to the extent that the payer jurisdiction allows the deduction in respect of the payment or deemed payment to be set off against an amount that is not dual-inclusion income.

The rules also capture double deduction outcomes regardless of whether they arise as a result of payments, expenses or losses in the payer or investor jurisdiction. A hybrid mismatch should only arise, however, to the extent that the payer jurisdiction allows the deduction to be set off against an amount that is not dual-inclusion income.

To counter imported mismatches, the rules disallow the deduction of a payment if the corresponding income from that payment is set off, directly or indirectly, against a deduction that arises under a hybrid mismatch giving rise to a double deduction or a deduction without inclusion.

Dual resident mismatches leading to double deduction outcomes also fall within the scope of the hybrid mismatch rules in CITA. The duplicate deduction arising in respect of a dual resident company is denied to the extent that this payment is set off against an amount that is not treated as dual inclusion income under the laws of the other jurisdiction.
